“Rebellion cannot do without the notion of a limit — it stops…” — Albert Camus (The Rebel)

Source and attribution

The archive attributes this English wording to The Rebel and files it under Philosophy of the Absurd. That locator distinguishes the passage from loose internet attributions: readers can return to the named work or section to check translation, surrounding argument, and edition-specific wording.

About Albert Camus

Albert Camus (1913–1960) was a French-Algerian writer and thinker associated with the absurd: the tension between the human demand for meaning and a world that does not supply it. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957 and rejected being labeled an existentialist in the Sartrean sense, while remaining central to twentieth-century debates about revolt, justice, and lucid living without appeal to transcendence.

How to read this passage

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, dignity.

Concepts in this quote

Knowledge
Knowledge is the philosophical study of what we can justifiably claim to know—and where certainty ends.
Dignity
Dignity names the worth that persons claim simply as persons—and the respect that worth demands.
